children: is investing in fusion startup Xcimer Energy as part of a roughly $50 million agreement to develop a laser weapon designed to destroy drones, missiles and other airborne threats, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

The companies plan to demonstrate a mobile prototype within two years. The ultraviolet laser system would be approximately the size of a shipping container and use electricity to fire repeated pulses, potentially giving military operators a far deeper supply of shots than conventional interceptors.

investors, the partnership provides exposure to a potentially cheaper answer to an increasingly expensive defense problem. Militaries often use missiles costing hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars to destroy comparatively inexpensive drones. An electrically powered laser could reduce the cost per engagement, although the system remains experimental and the $50 million project is unlikely to materially affect RTX’s near-term results. For privately held Xcimer, the agreement provides revenue and a defense application while it pursues the much longer-term goal of commercial fusion power.

will contribute tracking, targeting and command technology, while Denver-based Xcimer will develop the laser and its light source. The companies see the system as particularly useful against large groups of low-cost drones.
Cold War technology gets another shot

Xcimer’s approach revives concepts explored during President Ronald Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative. Researchers in the 1980s studied powerful gas-based excimer lasers as possible missile defenses, but government interest waned after the Cold War.
Founded in 2021, Xcimer has raised nearly $200 million from investors including Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Emerson Collective. It also received $9 million from the Department of Energy.

The startup uses gas-based lasers in its fusion research, an approach it believes could be less costly than the specialized glass lasers used at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The national laboratory achieved fusion ignition in 2022, producing more energy from the reaction than the laser energy delivered to the fuel target.

Xcimer ultimately aims to develop a commercial fusion power plant by 2035. Its work with RTX offers a more immediate market for the underlying laser technology, provided the prototype can prove effective outside the laboratory.
